passage: Joseph here. Tenzin, who sits opposite me, keeps a small notebook by her keyboard, and for two weeks I watched her write down start and end times for everything. I asked once. "My boxes are wrong," she said, "but I need the numbers first." On the second Friday she opened her schedule and changed it. The weekly report block went from one hour to ninety minutes, because her notes showed it never took less. After every meeting she put a fifteen-minute gap labelled "notes and messages", since she had been rushing into the next task with half-written follow-ups. Her week looked calmer after that, though I cannot say what she felt, only that she stopped skipping lunch. She told me the first week with the new boxes ended with everything sent on time.

Week one. Yamini started a small log beside her calendar at the Pune firm. Every task, what she had planned, and how long it actually took. The weekly report: planned one hour, took two and ten minutes. Client meetings: planned thirty minutes, usually forty-five, plus fifteen minutes of messages afterwards.
Week two. The pattern was the same every day. She showed her senior, Ganga, the log over tea. "My boxes are wrong. Not a little. The report is double."
"So what will you change?"
"Report block becomes two hours. And fifteen free minutes after every meeting, for the follow-ups."
Week four. Ganga stopped by her desk at 5.30. "You're packing up on time?"
"The day finally fits," Yamini said, showing her the calendar with its new gaps. "I'm not chasing my own schedule anymore."

qa.q: How long did the weekly report actually take?
qa.a: The weekly report took two hours and ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel by week four?
qa.a: She felt relieved and calmer, saying the day finally fits and she is no longer chasing her own schedule.

qa.q: What else could Yamini track to keep improving her schedule?
qa.a: She could keep the log for one day a month, since tasks may change and her boxes could drift out of date again.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Yamini's log?
qa.a: Ganga may be impressed that Yamini used real numbers to fix the schedule, and pleased to see her leaving on time.

grounding: It shows a woman noting how long tasks really take for two weeks, then lengthening her report block and adding fifteen free minutes after meetings.

passage:
Chandrika, you're always late with everything even though your calendar looks so neat. Your Sabina Phuppo made the same mistake at your age. Let me tell you.
My first job was at a hospital billing office. I made a beautiful timetable: forty-five minutes for the daily claims report, thirty minutes per meeting, no breaks between. Every day I was late. Every day I felt like a failure.
Then my supervisor gave me a small notebook. "For two weeks, write how long things really take. Don't change anything yet." So I did.
The claims report never took forty-five minutes. It took an hour and a half, every time. And after every meeting I needed fifteen minutes just to answer what came out of it.
So I changed my timetable. Report got ninety minutes. Every meeting got fifteen free minutes after it. And for the first time, I went home on time. Try the notebook, beta.

qa.q: How long did the claims report really take?
qa.a: It took an hour and a half, every time.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel before she started the notebook?
qa.a: Sabina felt ashamed and discouraged, like a failure, since she was late every day despite her neat timetable.

qa.q: When the supervisor gave her the notebook, what choice did Sabina make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She tracked for two weeks without changing anything first, so she could see the real times before fixing the plan.

qa.q: How might Sabina's supervisor have seen her new timetable?
qa.a: The supervisor would likely be pleased, seeing that the notebook led to a plan that finally fit the real work.

grounding: It shows a woman tracking how long tasks really take, then lengthening her report block and adding gaps after meetings.
